Empirical Research Plan: “Acquirer Size and Shareholder Wealth Gains in Takeovers, 1980-2001”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Step 1:  Event–study   –  Measure the causal effect of each acquisition announcement on the acquirer’s share-price (three-day cumulative abnormal return, CAR[-1,+1]).  This is standard because the announcement date is exogenous to the very short-run return and, under semi-strong market efficiency, CAR isolates the market’s assessment of net present value created by the deal.

Step 2:  Instrumental-variables (2SLS, cross-sectional) –  To study how ex-ante acquirer size affects those announcement returns, treat size as endogenous and use exogenous variation generated by Russell 1000/2000 index reconstitutions.  Near the annual cut-off (end-May), firms are assigned to the R2000 (small-cap) or R1000 (large-cap) essentially mechanically by rank in May market-capitalisation; that assignment moves index-fund demand and analyst attention but is orthogonal to firm fundamentals in the short run.  Because index assignment strongly predicts log-size one month later yet is determined outside the control of management, it is a powerful, plausibly valid instrument.

Why IV > simple OLS?
•  Larger firms differ systematically in governance, growth opportunities, and bargaining power – confounders that also affect CARs.
•  Russell assignment provides quasi-random shocks to “perceived size” that are not driven by those unobservables.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Main specification (continuous treatment):
  •  Endogenous variable: SIZE_i  = ln(MarketCap_i,-6)  (log of equity market value six trading days before announcement).
  •  Instrument:  R2000_i  = 1 if firm is a member of Russell 2000 at the June reconstitution immediately preceding the announcement year; 0 if in Russell 1000 and ‑90 ≤ Rank ≤ +90 around the cut-off (a ±90-rank “donut” window).

Binary robustness spec.:
  •  “Treated” = Small acquirer (bottom NYSE size quartile in its announcement year).
  •  “Control” = Large acquirer (top NYSE size quartile).
Event date: announcement date t = 0; CAR window [-1,+1].

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1  Efficient-market/no-leakage  – Share price fully reflects all publicly available information by t = +1 and is not contaminated by earlier leakage or confounding events.  Plausible because window is only three days; we drop deals with confounding announcements in [-5,+5].

A2  Instrument relevance  – Russell assignment substantially shifts log size.  Well documented (first-stage F > 100 in prior studies); we will report F-stat.

A3  Exclusion restriction  – Conditional on SIZE and controls, Russell membership affects CAR only through its impact on acquirer size, not through some other channel directly related to the value created by the particular acquisition.  Plausible because index reconstitution is unrelated to acquisition strategy; we will probe by showing no association with deal characteristics (method-of-payment, hostility, etc.).

A4  No selective compliance / monotonicity  – Firms cannot precisely manipulate their May market-cap rank to obtain a given index; literature finds no bunching at the cut-off.

A5  SUTVA  – Each acquirer’s CAR is unaffected by other firms’ index assignment during the three-day window.  Highly plausible.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
────────────────────────────────────────
T1  Sample-selection into “acquirers”                      
    –  Index assignment might influence the probability of making any acquisition.  
    • Fix: restrict analysis to firms that do announce at least one acquisition; include firm fixed effects when multiple deals occur in the same year; show no jump in acquisition propensity at cut-off.

T2  Violation of exclusion via liquidity / index demand    
    –  Russell membership changes stock-level liquidity and may itself alter returns during the CAR window.  
    • Fix: use a short estimation window that begins after the “reconstitution drift” has fully priced; add controls for abnormal turnover during [-30,-6]; replicate using dollar-CAR (which nets out price-impact effects).

T3  Remaining confounders correlated with size even after instrumentation  
    –  E.g., governance quality, cash holdings.  
    • Fix: include rich vector of firm and deal controls, industry × year FE; show that the IV coefficient is stable to adding those covariates.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# --------------------------------------------------
# 0. packages
# --------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)      # fast OLS/IV w/robust se
library(modelsummary)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 1. load data
# --------------------------------------------------
acq  <- read_csv("sdc_acquisitions_1980_2001.csv")   # deal-level SDC variables
russ <- read_csv("russell_membership.csv")           # firm-year Russell 1k/2k assignments
mkt  <- read_csv("crsp_daily.csv")                   # for abnormal-return estimation (if needed)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 2. variable construction
# --------------------------------------------------
acq <- acq %>% 
  mutate(ann_date    = ymd(ann_date),
         size_ln     = log(mktcap_tminus6),
         small_q1    = as.integer(size_percentile_nyse <= 25),
         car_3       = car_neg1_to_pos1,             # already pre-computed
         dollar_car  = car_3 * mktcap_tminus6)

# merge Russell classification from the *June* reconstitution before announcement
acq <- acq %>% 
  left_join(russ, by = c("permno","fyear")) %>%
  mutate(r2000      = as.integer(index == "R2000"),
         abs_rank   = abs(rank_distance))             # rank_distance = firm rank - cutoff rank

# restrict to tight window around cut-off for stronger first stage
acq <- acq %>% filter(abs_rank <= 90)                 # ±90 ranks (approx ±4%)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 3. main IV specification
# --------------------------------------------------
iv_eq <- feols(car_3 ~ 1 | size_ln ~ r2000 + controls(.), 
               data = acq,
               cluster = ~ann_year)                   # cluster by calendar year

etable(iv_eq, se = "cluster")

# --------------------------------------------------
# 4. OLS baseline for comparison
# --------------------------------------------------
ols_eq <- feols(car_3 ~ size_ln + controls(.), 
                data = acq, 
                cluster = ~ann_year)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 5. robustness: alternative outcome (dollar CAR)
# --------------------------------------------------
iv_dollar <- feols(dollar_car ~ 1 | size_ln ~ r2000 + controls(.), 
                   data = acq,
                   cluster = ~ann_year)

# helper: define control variables once
controls <- function(dot=.) { 
  fml <- ~ deal_value_rel + hostile + tender + comp_bid + cash_only + stock_only +
          private_target + subsidiary_target +
          q_ratio + leverage + cash_assets + ind_fe + year_fe
  update(dot, fml)
}
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Theory predicts that smaller acquirers should show larger positive CARs because:
  •  Managers own more equity (lower agency costs, less overpayment).
  •  Smaller firms are less likely to be overvalued (lower “hubris” problem).
  •  For private- and subsidiary targets, information frictions, not bargaining power, dominate.

Hence I expect:
  •  IV coefficient of ln(Size) on CAR ≈ ‑0.003 to ‑0.004  (i.e., a one-log-unit ↑ in size lowers the 3-day CAR by 30-40 bp).
  •  Economic magnitude: Moving from 25th- to 75th-percentile size (~2.5 log points) reduces CAR by roughly 0.9-1.0 percentage-points, which is close to the unconditional difference observed in previous samples (small ≈ +1.5 %, large ≈ +0.5 %).

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)
────────────────────────────────────────
1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable/absent

C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10)............................... 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction clearly justified........................... 0.5  
C3: No manipulation / continuity at cut-off........................... 1  
C4: SUTVA (no spillovers across firms during 3-day window)............ 1  
C5: Robust inference & multiple robustness checks..................... 1  

Total = 4.5 / 5 – overall high internal validity, primary caveat being the untestable exclusion restriction.
